parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a guesthouse in a hill town to book a room.
script: Good morning, Hillcrest Lodge, Raj speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book a room for next month, please.
Of course. Can I start with your name?
Yes, it's Ellen Fairbank. F, A, I, R, B, A, N, K.
Thank you. And when would you like to arrive?
I was planning to arrive on the twelfth of April, but my flight's been changed, so it'll be the thirteenth now.
So, arriving on the thirteenth. What kind of room would you like?
A double, please. And if possible, with a view of the mountains rather than the garden.
We have one mountain-view double left. It's on the top floor, and there's no lift, I'm afraid.
The garden-view rooms are eighty dollars a night, and the mountain-view ones are ninety-five, including breakfast.
Do you have any dietary requirements for breakfast?
No problem at all. How will you be travelling here?
By train. Is the lodge far from the station?
About twenty minutes by car. Our driver can collect you. He'll wait outside the ticket office, not on the platform, because the platform gets very crowded.
Great. My train gets in at two forty-five in the afternoon.
I'll let him know. We also run tours. There's a sunrise trip every morning, and a visit to a tea plantation, but the plantation trip is only on Thursdays.
Oh, I'll be there on a Thursday. I'd love to do that.
Wonderful. One more thing. The days are warm in April, but the evenings can be very cold up here, so please bring a warm jacket.
Finally, to confirm the booking, we ask for a deposit equal to the cost of one night.
That's fine. I can pay now by card.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A council officer talks on local radio about a new bike-sharing scheme.
script: Hello, and thanks for having me on the programme. I'm Joanna Lee from the city council's transport team, and I'm here to tell listeners about CityCycle, our new bike-sharing scheme, which launches on the first of June.

The idea for the scheme came from a survey of residents last year. We expected people to ask for more buses, but what came out most strongly was that people would cycle more if bikes were easy to pick up and drop off.

At launch there will be two hundred and fifty bikes at forty stations across the city. We'd originally planned sixty stations, but we decided it was better to start smaller and expand once we see how people use them.
Half of the bikes are electric, which should make a big difference on the steep hills in the north of the city.
To rent a bike, you'll need our mobile app. There are no ticket machines at the stations, so you register in the app and then scan the code on the bike.
On safety, we don't provide helmets, although we strongly recommend that you wear your own. But every bike has front and back lights that switch on automatically when it gets dark.

Now, prices. A single ride costs one pound for the first thirty minutes, and fifty pence for every extra fifteen minutes. If you cycle regularly, a monthly pass is much better value. We originally planned to charge twenty pounds for that, but after listening to residents we've set it at fifteen. Students and people over sixty-five pay half price.

Please remember to return bikes to a station. If you leave a bike anywhere else, you'll be charged a ten-pound fine. And if a bike is damaged, or you have any other problem, just press the help button in the app, and our team will respond within an hour.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Lucas and Hana, discuss their project on student volunteering.
script: Hana, have you had a chance to look at the sources for our volunteering project?
Yes. But first, I think our research question needs narrowing. 'Why young people volunteer' is far too broad. How about focusing on university students only?
Good idea. It's a more manageable topic.
What did you find most interesting in the reading?
That the main reason students volunteer isn't to improve their CV, which is what I'd assumed. Most of them say it's to meet people and feel part of a community.
For our survey, should we do it online or by interview?
Online gets more responses, but interviews give deeper answers. Why don't we do both? An online questionnaire first, then five follow-up interviews.
Fine. But response rates could be a problem. Last year's group only got thirty responses.
We could offer a small prize, like café vouchers.
Our tutor said incentives can bias the results. Let's ask lecturers to share the link at the start of their lectures instead.
OK. What worries you most about the project?
Analysing the interviews. Coding all those answers takes ages.
Right, let's go through the sources. The government report from 2009?
It's out of date. Volunteering has changed a lot since apps made it easier to sign up.
It's very readable, but it's too general. It covers people of all ages, not students.
The survey on the charity's website?
Remember the charity wants to recruit volunteers, so it may present things too positively. It could be biased.
What about the journal article by Okoye?
That's the most useful one. It has detailed statistics on students specifically.
Interesting, but it's about volunteering abroad, so it isn't really relevant to us.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of salt.
script: Today we're looking at a substance we hardly think about: salt. Yet for most of human history, salt was one of the most valuable goods in the world.
Why? Before refrigeration, salt was essential for preserving food, especially meat and fish. Without it, communities could not store food through the winter or carry it on long journeys.
Salt was so important that it shaped language. Roman soldiers were sometimes given money to buy salt, and many historians believe this is the origin of the English word salary.

Governments quickly realised that salt could be taxed. In ancient China, salt taxes provided a large share of state income, and some of this money is thought to have helped pay for the building of the Great Wall.

In West Africa, salt from the Sahara was so scarce in the south that it was traded for gold, sometimes weight for weight. It was carried across the desert by camel caravans, some with thousands of animals.
In Europe, the city of Venice grew rich from the salt trade, and used this wealth to build a powerful fleet of ships that dominated Mediterranean trade.

Salt has also been at the centre of political protest. In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led the famous Salt March to the sea, to protest against a British tax on salt in India. The march drew international attention to the independence movement.

Today, salt is cheap and plentiful. Surprisingly, only a small percentage of it is used in food. Most is used to keep roads free of ice in winter, and a great deal goes to industry, for example in the manufacture of plastics.
Finally, a word on health. Our bodies need some salt, but too much raises blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart disease and strokes.

passages.title: The Great Green Wall
paragraphs: South of the Sahara Desert lies the Sahel, a belt of semi-arid land stretching across Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea. For decades, the region has suffered from drought, overgrazing and the loss of trees, and millions of people who depend on farming and herding have seen their land become less productive. In 2007 the African Union launched an ambitious response: the Great Green Wall.

The original vision was striking in its simplicity. A continuous line of trees, around 15 kilometres wide and almost 8,000 kilometres long, would be planted from Senegal in the west to Djibouti in the east, holding back the advance of the desert. Eleven countries signed up, and international donors pledged billions of dollars. The project's target is to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.

Progress, however, has been slow. A 2020 assessment found that only around four percent of the target area had been restored. In many places, trees were planted in large numbers by government agencies but not looked after, and in some regions most of the seedlings died within a few years. Critics also pointed out that the idea of a 'wall' misunderstood the problem: deserts do not advance like an army, and land becomes degraded mainly because of how it is used.

Some of the most impressive results have come not from planting but from protecting what was already there. In Niger in the 1980s, the Australian agronomist Tony Rinaudo noticed that many apparently dead fields were full of living tree stumps, whose roots were still alive below ground. He encouraged farmers to select the strongest shoots growing from these stumps, protect them from animals and prune them carefully. The technique, known as farmer-managed natural regeneration, costs very little and requires no expensive equipment. It has since spread to around five million hectares in Niger alone.

The benefits go well beyond holding the soil in place. Trees provide shade for crops, fodder for animals and firewood for cooking, and their fallen leaves enrich the soil. In Senegal, farmers have planted acacia trees that produce gum arabic, a valuable ingredient used in food and medicine, giving families a new source of income.

Today, the Great Green Wall is rarely described as a wall at all. Instead, its supporters talk of a mosaic of different land uses, including restored forests, farmland, grazing areas and water-harvesting projects, chosen by local communities to suit local conditions. Whether the 2030 target can be met remains doubtful, but the project has shown that the Sahel's future does not have to be one of retreat.

passages.title: A Short History of Paper Money
paragraphs: Most of us accept paper notes and digital balances without a second thought, yet the idea behind them is remarkable. A banknote has almost no value as a material object; it is worth something only because everyone trusts that others will accept it. The history of paper money is, in many ways, a history of how that trust was built, and how easily it could be lost.

The first steps were taken in China. During the Tang dynasty, in the ninth century, merchants travelling long distances found it impractical to carry large quantities of copper coins. Instead, they deposited their coins with agents in one city and received paper receipts, which could be exchanged for coins in another. Because these receipts seemed to travel without effort, they became known as 'flying money'.

True paper currency appeared in the province of Sichuan in the early eleventh century, during the Song dynasty. Sichuan used iron coins, which were so heavy and of such low value that buying a single roll of silk required a large load of metal. Private shops began issuing paper notes, called jiaozi, in exchange for deposits of coins. After several shops failed and could not repay their customers, the government took over the system in 1023, creating the world's first government-issued paper money.

The advantages were obvious, but so were the dangers. When the Mongols ruled China as the Yuan dynasty, they made paper the main form of money throughout the empire. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo described with astonishment how the emperor could produce money simply by printing it. But that was precisely the problem: governments facing heavy costs printed more and more notes, prices rose rapidly, and by the fifteenth century the Ming dynasty had largely abandoned paper money.

Europe was slow to follow. The first European banknotes were issued in 1661 by Stockholms Banco in Sweden, but the bank issued far more notes than it could repay and collapsed within a few years. More lasting success came with the Bank of England, founded in 1694, whose notes could be exchanged for gold. For more than two centuries, the link to gold reassured the public that paper money had real value.

That link has now disappeared. Since 1971, when the United States ended the exchange of dollars for gold, the world's major currencies have been backed by nothing more than the authority of governments and the confidence of the people who use them. Meanwhile, cash itself is declining, as payments move to cards and phones, and several central banks are developing digital currencies. The form of money continues to change, but the principle discovered by Chinese merchants a thousand years ago remains the same: money works only as long as we believe in it.

passages.title: In Defence of Boredom
paragraphs: Few experiences are as widely disliked as boredom. We complain about boring meetings, boring journeys and boring jobs, and we have built an entire industry of devices and apps designed to make sure that we never have to feel it. Smartphones allow us to escape boredom at any moment, whether we are waiting for a bus or standing in a queue. But a growing body of research suggests that, in our hurry to eliminate boredom, we may be losing something valuable.

It is worth being clear about what boredom is. It is not simply having nothing to do; people can be bored in the middle of a busy day. Psychologists such as James Danckert describe it as the feeling of wanting to be engaged in something satisfying while being unable to find it. In this sense, boredom acts as a signal, much like pain or hunger, telling us that our current activity is not meeting our needs and that we should change what we are doing. Seen this way, it is a useful emotion rather than a purely unpleasant one.

Some studies suggest that boredom may also encourage creativity. In a 2014 experiment by the psychologists Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman, one group of participants was first asked to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers out of a telephone directory, a deliberately dull task. They were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with a group that had not done the boring task, they came up with more ideas. The researchers suggested that boredom leads the mind to wander, and that daydreaming may help the brain to make new connections between ideas. Such findings should be treated with caution, since the studies are small, but they are consistent with many artists' accounts of their own working habits.

Our discomfort with boredom can be surprisingly strong. In a well-known study led by Timothy Wilson, participants were asked to sit alone in a room with nothing to do for up to fifteen minutes. Beforehand, they had been given the option of pressing a button to give themselves a mild electric shock. Many of them, particularly the men, chose to shock themselves rather than simply sit with their thoughts. It seems that, for many people, being alone with one's mind is an experience to be avoided at almost any cost.

None of this means that boredom is always good. Researchers distinguish between the occasional experience of being bored and 'trait boredom', a long-term tendency to feel bored easily and often. Trait boredom has been linked to depression, overeating and risky behaviour such as gambling. For people who experience it, boredom is not a gentle push towards creativity but a persistent source of distress.

In my view, the lesson is not that we should seek out boredom, but that we should stop treating it as an enemy to be defeated. When we reach for a phone the moment we feel restless, we miss the signal that boredom provides and the opportunity it offers for reflection. For children in particular, the answer is not to make every moment entertaining. I believe parents and schools should allow children some unstructured time, in which they must find their own ways to occupy themselves. Learning to deal with boredom may be one of the more useful skills a young person can acquire.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the number of international students, in thousands, studying in five countries in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the number of international students in the USA, the UK, Australia, Canada and Germany in 2010 and 2020.
Overall, all five countries attracted more international students over the decade. The USA remained by far the most popular destination, while Canada recorded the most dramatic growth.

In 2010, the USA hosted 720,000 international students, almost twice as many as the UK, which had 400,000. Australia had 240,000, Germany 180,000 and Canada just 130,000, the lowest figure of the five.

By 2020, the number in the USA had risen to one million. The UK also saw an increase, to 550,000, but the most striking change was in Canada, where numbers almost quadrupled to 500,000, overtaking Australia. Australia's figure nearly doubled, reaching 460,000, while Germany's rose more modestly, to 300,000, leaving it in last place.

task2.text: Some people believe that parents should strictly limit the amount of time children spend using phones, tablets and computers. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: Digital devices have become a central part of childhood, and many parents worry about how much time their children spend looking at screens. I agree that parents should set clear limits, although I believe these limits should be sensible rather than strict, and should depend on how the devices are used.

There are good reasons for limiting screen time. Excessive use is linked to poor sleep, especially when children use phones late at night, and to a lack of physical activity, which can affect health. Many apps and games are also designed to be addictive, so children, whose self-control is still developing, may find it difficult to stop on their own. Without limits, screens can easily replace reading, outdoor play and face-to-face conversation, all of which are important for development.

However, extremely strict rules can be counterproductive. Much schoolwork is now done online, and digital skills are essential for future careers. Moreover, not all screen time is equal: a child video-calling grandparents, coding a simple game or watching a documentary is doing something very different from scrolling endlessly through short videos. Rules that treat all screen use as harmful may simply lead children to hide their use or rebel against their parents.

In my view, the most effective approach is for parents to agree limits with their children, focusing on the type of content as well as the amount of time. Simple rules, such as no devices at meals or in bedrooms at night, are easier to follow than complicated timetables.
In conclusion, I agree that parents should limit their children's screen time, but these limits work best when they are reasonable, consistent and based on how devices are used.

speaking.cue:
Describe a journey you remember well.
You should say:
- where you went
- how you travelled
- who you were with
and explain why you remember this journey.
speaking.cueModel: The journey I remember best is a train trip from Dhaka to Sylhet that I took with my family a few years ago, when I'd just finished my school exams. We'd usually travelled by bus before, so taking the train felt like a small adventure. We left early in the morning, and the journey took about seven hours. What made it memorable was the scenery. Once we left the city, the view changed to bright green rice fields, and then, as we got closer to Sylhet, to rolling hills covered in tea gardens. I spent most of the trip standing by the window taking photos. There were also people selling tea and snacks in every carriage, and my father, who normally never chats to strangers, ended up having a long conversation with a retired teacher sitting opposite us. I think I remember it so well because it was the first holiday after a very stressful period of studying, so I felt completely free. It also made me realise that the journey itself can be just as enjoyable as the destination.
